EMERGENCY (EX PARTE) CUSTODY ORDER — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

DECLARATION IN SUPPORT OF AN EX PARTE APPLICATION FOR EMERGENCY CUSTODY ORDERS
I, Jordan Alex Lee, declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the following is true and correct. I am a party to a pending or about-to-be-filed family law case in San Francisco County concerning the custody of the following child or children: Casey Lee, age 7. The other parent is Taylor Morgan. I am considering an ex parte application for emergency orders under California Rules of Court, rule 5.151 and Family Code section 3064, requesting a temporary custody or visitation order without a full noticed hearing. The most recent incident(s) I believe show immediate harm to the child or an immediate risk that the child will be removed from the State of California, including the date(s) of each incident, are described as follows: the other parent has threatened to remove the child from California without notice. The most recent such incident occurred on or about August 28, 2026. This declaration is prepared for use alongside the actual Judicial Council forms required by California Rules of Court, rule 5.151(c) -- including a Request for Order (form FL-300), a proposed Temporary Emergency (Ex Parte) Orders (form FL-305), and a declaration regarding notice (form FL-303 or its equivalent) -- filed with the California superior court handling the case. It is not itself a court filing, and completing it does not grant, deny, or constitute an emergency custody order. Whether the facts described here meet Family Code section 3064's immediate-harm-or-immediate-risk-of-removal standard is a determination only the court can make.

EX PARTE APPLICATION PROCEDURE AND STANDARD UNDER CALIFORNIA RULES OF COURT, RULE 5.151
California Rules of Court, rule 5.151 governs applications for emergency orders -- also called ex parte applications -- in family law cases. Rule 5.151(b) states that the purpose of a request for emergency orders is to address matters that cannot wait for the court's regular hearing calendar, that notice to the other party is shorter than in other family law proceedings, and that notice can be waived under exceptional and other circumstances stated in the rule. An ex parte request for emergency orders is not limited to custody; rule 5.151(b) describes its use to prevent immediate danger or irreparable harm to a party or to the children involved, to prevent immediate loss or damage to property subject to disposition in the case, and to address certain procedural matters such as shortening time for a hearing. Rule 5.151(d)(2) states the general factual showing required: the declarations supporting the application must contain facts within the declarant's personal knowledge that demonstrate why the matter is appropriately handled as an emergency, and the applicant must make an affirmative factual showing of irreparable harm, immediate danger, or another statutory basis for granting relief without notice or with shortened notice. Rule 5.151(d)(5) states that an application for emergency orders granting or modifying child custody or visitation must specifically be made under Family Code section 3064 and must include a full, detailed description of the most recent incidents showing immediate harm to the child (as defined in section 3064(b)) or immediate risk that the child will be removed from California, the date of each such incident, the existing custody and visitation arrangements and how the request would change them, a copy of any current custody order (or an explanation of where and with whom the child currently lives if none exists), and a completed UCCJEA declaration (form FL-105). Rule 5.151(c) lists the required documents for any request for emergency orders, including a Request for Order (form FL-300), a proposed order (form FL-305), and a written declaration regarding notice (form FL-303 or its equivalent).

Notice to the other party can also be waived under exceptional and other circumstances as provided in these rules."
  — Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.151(b), purpose of an ex parte application for emergency orders and shortened/waivable notice (https://courts.ca.gov/cms/rules/index/five/rule5_151)
  "An applicant must make an affirmative factual showing of irreparable harm, immediate danger, or any other statutory basis for granting relief without notice or with shortened notice to the other party."
  — Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.151(d)(2), the affirmative factual showing required (https://courts.ca.gov/cms/rules/index/five/rule5_151)

This clause states what the rule provides; it does not itself grant, deny, or constitute an emergency order, and it does not tell any specific reader whether their situation meets the rule's showing requirement -- only a court, applying the rule to a specific application, can make that determination.

FAMILY CODE SECTION 3064: THE IMMEDIATE-HARM STANDARD FOR AN EX PARTE CUSTODY ORDER
Family Code section 3064(a) states the specific limiting standard for ex parte custody relief: the court shall refrain from granting or modifying a custody order on an ex parte basis unless there has been a showing of immediate harm to the child or immediate risk that the child will be removed from the State of California. Section 3064(b)(1) defines "immediate harm to the child" to include, without limitation, having a parent who has committed acts of domestic violence of recent origin or as part of a demonstrated and continuing pattern, or sexual abuse of the child of recent origin or as part of a demonstrated and continuing pattern. Section 3064(b)(2)(A) additionally requires the court, in determining whether immediate harm has been shown, to consider a parent's illegal access to firearms and ammunition, including whether that parent is prohibited from having firearms and ammunition. As fetched and verified, section 3064's text does not condition ex parte custody relief on a finding that the request is not sought merely to alter jurisdiction or venue; no such jurisdiction- or venue-focused limitation appears anywhere in the statutory text of section 3064.

NOTICE OF THE EX PARTE APPLICATION ITSELF: CALIFORNIA RULES OF COURT, RULE 5.165
Ex parte does not mean no notice at all under California's general emergency-orders rules; California Rules of Court, rule 5.165(b) states that a party seeking emergency orders under this chapter must give notice to all parties or their attorneys so that it is received no later than 10:00 a.m. on the court day before the matter is to be considered by the court. If notice is given later than that deadline, rule 5.165(b)(1) requires the party to request, in a declaration regarding notice, that the court approve the shortened notice, supported by facts showing exceptional circumstances. Separately, rule 5.165(b)(2) allows a party to ask the court to waive notice entirely, by filing a written declaration signed under penalty of perjury showing good cause; the rule lists five categories of good cause a judicial officer may rely on: that giving notice would frustrate the purpose of the order; that giving notice would result in immediate and irreparable harm to the applicant or the children who may be affected; that giving notice would result in immediate and irreparable damage to or loss of property subject to disposition in the case; that the parties agreed in advance that notice would not be necessary; or that the party made reasonable, good-faith efforts to give notice and further efforts would probably be futile or unduly burdensome. Rule 5.165(b) also states that this notice rule does not apply to a party seeking emergency orders under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act.

THE FOLLOW-UP NOTICED HEARING AFTER AN EX PARTE CUSTODY ORDER
Family Code section 3062, not section 3066, is the provision requiring a further noticed hearing after an ex parte custody order. Section 3062(a) states that, absent an agreement, understanding, or stipulation between the parties, the court may -- if jurisdiction is appropriate -- enter an ex parte temporary custody order, set a hearing date within 20 days, and issue an order to show cause on the responding party; if the responding party does not appear or respond within the time set, the temporary order may be extended as necessary pending termination of the proceedings. Section 3062(b) states that if service of the ex parte order and order to show cause has not been timely effected despite good-faith efforts, and there is reason to believe the responding party has possession of the child and seeks to avoid the court's jurisdiction or is concealing the child's whereabouts, the hearing date may be reset and the ex parte order extended up to an additional 90 days; after service is effected, either party may request ex parte that the hearing date be advanced or the ex parte order be dissolved or modified. Family Code section 3063 separately states that in conjunction with any ex parte order seeking or modifying custody, the court shall enter an order restraining the person receiving custody from removing the child from the state, pending notice and a hearing on the underlying custody request. Both section 3062 and section 3064 (the immediate-harm standard) sit within the same statutory chapter, Family Code chapter 3 of division 8, part 2, titled 'Temporary Custody Order During Pendency of Proceeding,' spanning sections 3060 through 3064.

RELATIONSHIP TO A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE RESTRAINING ORDER: A SEPARATE PROCEDURAL TRACK
An ex parte request for emergency custody orders in a family law case under California Rules of Court, rule 5.151 and Family Code section 3064 is a separate procedural track from a request for a domestic violence restraining order under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (DVPA), which this corpus's separate Domestic Violence Restraining Order (Request for Order) Information Sheet document describes. Rule 5.151(a) states directly that the rules governing ex parte applications in family law cases -- described in this document -- do not apply to ex parte applications for domestic violence restraining orders under the DVPA, unless specifically stated otherwise. Rule 5.165(b) states the same distinction for its notice requirements: that rule does not apply to a party seeking emergency orders under the DVPA. The two tracks use different Judicial Council forms, different statutory standards (Family Code section 3064's immediate-harm-or-immediate-risk-of-removal standard for a custody-focused ex parte order under this document, versus the DVPA's own statutory abuse definition and ex parte mechanism for a DVRO), and different notice rules. The underlying facts prompting either request can overlap -- for example, a recent act of domestic violence can be relevant to both an ex parte custody request under section 3064(b)(1)(A) and a DVPA petition -- and a party may pursue either track, or both, depending on the circumstances of a specific case. Which track, or combination of tracks, applies to a specific set of facts is a legal determination; this document states the factual distinction between the two tracks and does not make that determination for any individual case.

BRIEF DISTINCTION: THE LAW-ENFORCEMENT-INITIATED EMERGENCY PROTECTIVE ORDER
A further, distinct emergency mechanism exists outside both tracks described above: the Emergency Protective Order (EPO) under Family Code section 6250. Section 6250 states that a judicial officer may issue an ex parte emergency protective order where a law enforcement officer asserts reasonable grounds to believe, among other things, that a person is in immediate and present danger of domestic violence, that a child is in immediate and present danger of abuse by a family or household member, or that a child is in immediate and present danger of being abducted by a parent or relative. Unlike the family-court ex parte custody procedure described in this document, an EPO is requested by a law enforcement officer, typically responding to an incident, directly to a judicial officer -- often by telephone -- rather than filed as a written application by a party or attorney in a pending or new family law case. An EPO is also short in duration: Family Code section 6256 states that an EPO expires at the earlier of two points, one measured in court days and one in calendar days from issuance.

Section 3062(a) states that, absent an agreement, understanding, or stipulation between the parties, the court may -- if jurisdiction is appropriate -- enter an ex parte temporary custody order, set a hearing date within 20 days, and issue an order to show cause on the responding party; if the responding party does not appear or respond within the time set, the temporary order may be extended as necessary pending termination of the proceedings. Section 3062(b) states that if service of the ex parte order and order to show cause has not been timely effected despite good-faith efforts, and there is reason to believe the responding party has possession of the child and seeks to avoid the court's jurisdiction or is concealing the child's whereabouts, the hearing date may be reset and the ex parte order extended up to an additional 90 days; after service is effected, either party may request ex parte that the hearing date be advanced or the ex parte order be dissolved or modified. Family Code section 3063 separately states that in conjunction with any ex parte order seeking or modifying custody, the court shall enter an order restraining the person receiving custody from removing the child from the state, pending notice and a hearing on the underlying custody request. Both section 3062 and section 3064 (the immediate-harm standard) sit within the same statutory chapter, Family Code chapter 3 of division 8, part 2, titled 'Temporary Custody Order During Pendency of Proceeding,' spanning sections 3060 through 3064.

An EPO is also short in duration: Family Code section 6256 states that an EPO expires at the earlier of two points, one measured in court days and one in calendar days from issuance.
